blocks.text:
On this journey, city tours alternate with Patagonia, glaciers, subtropical forest and the ocean coast. In Santiago, the focus is on history and modern architecture; in Patagonia, on open landscapes, granite peaks and ice; in Buenos Aires, on old neighbourhoods and tango; and in Rio, on viewpoints, beaches and mountains.

## Pace and structure of the journey

The first 2 days give you time to settle into South America before moving on to longer nature excursions. After arrival in Santiago, you have free time, followed the next day by a relaxed introduction to the historic centre and the modern part of the capital. An optional winery visit in the Maipo Valley can add a gastronomic element to the start of the trip if you have the energy for another outing after your flight.

On Day 3, the long journey to Patagonia begins. The flight to Punta Arenas, the bus to Puerto Natales and the subsequent excursion to Torres del Paine reveal how different the south is from Santiago. Dense urban development gives way to open steppe, lakes, cold winds and mountain massifs visible from afar. Milodón Cave and Salto Grande add specific stops and short walks to the panoramic scenery.

El Calafate continues this part of the journey, but ice takes over from granite towers as the main attraction. The town serves as a base on Lago Argentino, and the following day is devoted entirely to Perito Moreno. The glacier is constantly moving, something you can sense from the viewing platforms: you hear the cracking, see pieces fall into the water and watch the ice wall change appearance with each viewpoint.

After Patagonia, Buenos Aires feels especially vivid. One day takes you along grand avenues and through old neighbourhoods, ending with a tango show in the evening. The following day is deliberately left free. You can spend it in the city, discover rural Argentina at a Fiesta Gaucha, cross to Uruguay to visit Montevideo or head to the Tigre Delta. These excursions differ in both atmosphere and duration, making it easy to tailor the day to your interests.

Iguazu offers 2 different perspectives. The Argentine side involves more walking and lets you follow the Lower and Upper Circuits, approaching different cascades. The Brazilian side offers a sweeping panorama. This is also where you will find Macuco Safari, the helicopter departure point and the Bird Park. If you wish, you can turn one day into an extended nature excursion combining jungle, river and an aerial view of the falls.

The final days in Rio are more relaxed. First comes Sugar Loaf, then Corcovado and the historic city centre, followed by a free day. You can simply stroll around Copacabana, Leblon and Ipanema, or add the Botanical Garden, Petrópolis, a samba show or a short helicopter flight. The end of the trip stays flexible before your international departure.

## Details to bear in mind

In Santiago, the optional Maipo Valley excursion requires a minimum of 2 people. It is a separate outing in addition to the main city tour, so it is best planned when your flight schedule leaves enough time. The main city tour already includes Plaza de Armas, La Moneda, Santa Lucía Hill and the modern eastern part of the city.

In Patagonia, travel between places is a significant part of the experience. Between Puerto Natales and El Calafate, you cross into another country and a different natural landscape. The roads run through open steppe, providing plenty of views along the way. The day in Torres del Paine is long but includes several stops, while at Perito Moreno most of your time is spent on the network of walkways and viewing platforms.

It helps to think of the free day in Buenos Aires as a choice between different experiences. Fiesta Gaucha takes a full day and focuses on rural culture. Montevideo involves a ferry crossing and adds another country to the journey. Tigre requires less travel and centres on the delta islands, a boat trip and the northern suburbs.

Expect plenty of walking at Iguazu. The Argentine trails have specific lengths: the Lower Circuit is about 1,700 m, the Upper Circuit about 1,300 m, and the walk from the station to Devil’s Throat is about another 1,000 m. The Brazilian side involves less walking, and it is easier to combine Macuco, a helicopter flight and the Bird Park into one full day there.

In Rio, the optional activities vary considerably in duration. The Botanical Garden and samba show each take about 4 hours, a helicopter flight lasts less than 10 minutes, and Petrópolis requires a separate trip into the mountains, about 60 km from the city. You can therefore shape the final free day to suit your pace without changing the main tour programme.
